questionText: Which Italian friar and mathematician published the first systematic treatise on Double Entry Book-Keeping in Venice in 1494?

options.text: J. R. Batliboi
Luca De Bargo Pacioli
R. N. Carter
F. W. Taylor

explanation: Fra Luca De Bargo Pacioli, an Italian friar of Venice, outlined the principles of Double Entry Book-Keeping in his 1494 work Summa de Arithmetica (De Computis et Scripturis).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Introduction to Book-Keeping and Accountancy

questionText: How is a Trade Discount treated in the books of accounts at the time of recording a purchase or sale?

options.text: It is recorded only when the customer settles the account in cash
It is shown on the credit side of the Profit and Loss Account
It is debited to Trade Discount Account in the Journal
It is deducted from the catalogue price on the invoice and is not recorded separately in the books of accounts

explanation: Trade discount is an allowance granted on the list or catalogue price to boost bulk trade; purchases and sales are recorded directly at net invoice value without opening a Trade Discount Account.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Introduction to Book-Keeping and Accountancy

questionText: Which qualitative characteristic of accounting information enables stakeholders to evaluate performance trends of the same enterprise across multiple years as well as against rival firms?

options.text: Comparability
Conservatism
Materiality
Solvency

explanation: Comparability ensures that financial statements follow consistent conventions so users can perform both intra-firm (over time) and inter-firm comparisons.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Introduction to Book-Keeping and Accountancy

questionText: Goods with a list price of ₹80,000 are sold at a 10% trade discount and a 5% cash discount. If the buyer pays 60% of the net invoice value immediately by cheque, what is the amount of Cash Discount allowed?
explanation: Net invoice value after 10% trade discount = ₹80,000 − ₹8,000 = ₹72,000. Immediate settlement covers 60% of ₹72,000 = ₹43,200. Cash discount applies only to the settled portion: 5% of ₹43,200 = ₹2,160.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Introduction to Book-Keeping and Accountancy

questionText: A sole trader values unsold inventory at ₹1,32,000 (net realisable market value) rather than its historical cost of ₹1,45,000. Which accounting principle mandates this policy?

options.text: Conservatism (Prudence) Concept
Dual Aspect Concept
Going Concern Concept
Money Measurement Concept

explanation: The Conservatism (Prudence) principle states 'anticipate no profit, but provide for all possible losses', requiring closing stock to be valued at cost or market price whichever is lower.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Introduction to Book-Keeping and Accountancy

questionText: Immediately after purchasing a second-hand delivery tempo, a merchant spends ₹45,000 on complete engine reconditioning before using it for business deliveries. How should the ₹45,000 outlay be classified?

options.text: Contingent Liability
Revenue Expenditure
Deferred Revenue Receipt
Capital Expenditure

explanation: Any expenditure incurred on a newly acquired second-hand fixed asset to bring it into initial working condition increases its earning capacity and is capitalised as Capital Expenditure.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Introduction to Book-Keeping and Accountancy

questionText: Rakesh, a debtor owing ₹60,000, is adjudicated insolvent and only 35 paise in a rupee is recovered as first and final dividend from his official receiver. What amount must be written off as Bad Debts?
explanation: Amount recovered = ₹60,000 × 0.35 = ₹21,000. The irrecoverable portion written off as Bad Debts = ₹60,000 − ₹21,000 = ₹39,000.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Introduction to Book-Keeping and Accountancy

questionText: A commerce academy collects ₹3,60,000 upfront on 1st December 2025 for a 6-month training batch running from December 2025 through May 2026. If its financial year ends on 31st March 2026, how should this receipt be reported under the Accrual Concept?

options.text: ₹1,80,000 as earned revenue and ₹1,80,000 as capital reserve
Entire ₹3,60,000 deferred to FY 2026-27 when the batch concludes
₹2,40,000 as earned revenue for FY 2025-26 and ₹1,20,000 as unearned fee liability
Entire ₹3,60,000 as earned revenue in FY 2025-26 because cash was collected

explanation: Monthly fee = ₹3,60,000 ÷ 6 = ₹60,000. Four months (Dec 2025 to Mar 2026) fall in FY 2025-26, so ₹2,40,000 is recognised as revenue, while April–May 2026 (₹1,20,000) is carried as Income Received in Advance.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Introduction to Book-Keeping and Accountancy

questionText: A trader discounts a customer's Bill Receivable of ₹95,000 with his bank in February 2026; the bill matures on 15th May 2026. How should this unmatured discounted bill be disclosed on 31st March 2026?

options.text: As an Intangible Asset on the Assets side of the Balance Sheet
As a short-term liability inside the Liabilities column of the Balance Sheet
As Bad Debts on the debit side of the Profit and Loss Account
As a Contingent Liability by way of a footnote below the Balance Sheet

explanation: Liability on a discounted bill arises only if the acceptor dishonours it on the future due date (15th May 2026). Hence on 31st March 2026 it is a Contingent Liability shown as a Balance Sheet footnote.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Introduction to Book-Keeping and Accountancy

questionText: Samarth Printers buys a new offset press for ₹4,00,000, pays ₹12,000 for transit insurance, spends ₹18,000 on concrete foundation and installation wages, and pays ₹9,000 for an annual fire insurance policy after commissioning. What total amount is capitalised as Capital Expenditure?
explanation: All costs up to making the asset ready for intended use are capitalised: ₹4,00,000 + ₹12,000 (transit insurance) + ₹18,000 (installation) = ₹4,30,000. Post-commissioning annual fire insurance (₹9,000) is a recurring Revenue Expenditure.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 1: Introduction to Book-Keeping and Accountancy

questionText: Under the Traditional Approach of Double Entry Book-Keeping, what is the golden rule governing Real Accounts?

options.text: Debit all expenses and losses; Credit all incomes and gains
Debit all liabilities; Credit all assets
Debit what comes in; Credit what goes out
Debit the receiver; Credit the giver

explanation: Real accounts represent tangible and intangible assets/properties of a business, governed by the rule 'Debit what comes in; Credit what goes out'.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Meaning and Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping

questionText: Under the traditional classification of accounts, how is 'Prepaid Insurance Account' classified?

options.text: Representative Personal Account
Natural Personal Account
Nominal Account
Intangible Real Account

explanation: When a prefix or suffix like Outstanding, Prepaid, Accrued, or Received in Advance is added to a nominal item, it represents the person(s) to or from whom money is due, making it a Representative Personal Account.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Meaning and Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping

chapter: Meaning and Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping
questionText: According to the Modern Approach to accounting rules, which pair of account categories increases with a Debit entry and decreases with a Credit entry?

options.text: Assets and Revenues/Gains
Assets and Expenses/Losses
Liabilities and Capital
Capital and Expenses/Losses

explanation: Under the Modern Approach, Assets and Expenses/Losses carry normal debit balances—increases are debited and decreases are credited—whereas Liabilities, Capital, and Revenues increase on credit.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Meaning and Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping

chapter: Meaning and Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping
questionText: If a proprietary firm has Total Assets of ₹5,40,000 and External Liabilities of ₹1,85,000, what is the amount of Owner's Capital?
explanation: By the Accounting Equation (Assets = Liabilities + Capital), Capital = ₹5,40,000 − ₹1,85,000 = ₹3,55,000.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Meaning and Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping

chapter: Meaning and Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping
questionText: Which of the following pairs correctly matches an account with its exact traditional classification?

options.text: Copyright Account — Artificial Personal Account
Bank of Maharashtra Account — Tangible Real Account
Goodwill Account — Intangible Real Account
Drawings Account — Nominal Account

explanation: Goodwill, patents, trademarks, and copyrights are valuable business properties without physical form and are classified as Intangible Real Accounts; banks are Artificial Personal and Drawings is Personal.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Meaning and Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping

chapter: Meaning and Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping
topic: Accounting Equation — Profit on Credit Sale
questionText: Goods costing ₹28,000 are sold on credit to Meera for ₹35,000. What is the net effect on the Accounting Equation?

options.text: Total Assets increase by ₹35,000, Liabilities increase by ₹28,000, and Capital increases by ₹7,000
Total Assets increase by ₹7,000, Liabilities remain unchanged, and Capital increases by ₹7,000
Total Assets remain unchanged because Stock falls and Debtors rise equally
Total Assets increase by ₹7,000 and External Liabilities increase by ₹7,000

explanation: Stock decreases by ₹28,000 while Sundry Debtors increase by ₹35,000, yielding a net Asset increase of ₹7,000. The ₹7,000 profit accrues to the proprietor, increasing Capital by ₹7,000.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Meaning and Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping

chapter: Meaning and Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping
questionText: In a firm's books under the Modern Approach, under which category is 'Bank Overdraft Account' classified and how is a repayment toward reducing the overdraft recorded?

options.text: Liability Account — Debited when the overdraft is reduced
Expense Account — Debited when the overdraft is reduced
Capital Account — Credited when the overdraft is reduced
Asset Account — Credited when the overdraft is reduced

explanation: Bank Overdraft represents short-term borrowing owed to the bank (a Liability). Under Modern rules, decreases in liabilities are recorded by debiting the Liability Account.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Meaning and Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping

chapter: Meaning and Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping
questionText: Aarav starts business with Cash ₹2,00,000 and Furniture ₹50,000. He buys goods on credit from Kunal for ₹80,000, sells half of those goods for ₹52,000 cash, and then settles Kunal's account in full by paying ₹77,500 cash. What are the final values of Total Assets and Capital?

options.text: Total Assets ₹2,64,500 and Capital ₹2,59,500
Total Assets ₹2,62,000 and Capital ₹2,62,000
Total Assets ₹3,42,000 and Capital ₹2,64,500
Total Assets ₹2,64,500 and Capital ₹2,64,500

explanation: Initial Capital = ₹2,50,000. Selling half the goods (cost ₹40,000) for ₹52,000 yields ₹12,000 profit (Capital = ₹2,62,000). Settling ₹80,000 creditor for ₹77,500 yields ₹2,500 discount gain and eliminates liabilities. Final Capital = ₹2,64,500 = Total Assets (Cash ₹1,74,500 + Stock ₹40,000 + Furniture ₹50,000).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Meaning and Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping

chapter: Meaning and Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping
questionText: During a 12-month financial year, a shop paid ₹66,000 towards uniform monthly shop rent covering 11 months, leaving March's rent unpaid. What is the effect of recording the 12th month's unpaid rent on the Accounting Equation?

options.text: Total Assets decrease by ₹6,000 and Capital decreases by ₹6,000
Liabilities increase by ₹6,000, Capital decreases by ₹6,000, and Total Assets remain unchanged
Liabilities increase by ₹5,500 and Capital decreases by ₹5,500
Total Assets decrease by ₹6,000 and Liabilities increase by ₹6,000

explanation: Monthly rent = ₹66,000 ÷ 11 = ₹6,000. Recording unpaid March rent creates an Outstanding Rent liability (+₹6,000) and charges expense against Capital (−₹6,000), with no immediate cash outflow.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Meaning and Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping

chapter: Meaning and Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping
questionText: During the year, a proprietor brings her personal car valued at ₹3,20,000 into business use and later withdraws goods costing ₹14,000 (marked selling price ₹18,000) for household consumption. Ignoring other transactions, what is the net change in Capital?

options.text: Net increase of ₹3,20,000
Net increase of ₹3,34,000
Net increase of ₹3,06,000
Net increase of ₹3,02,000

explanation: Bringing a personal car into business adds ₹3,20,000 as Additional Capital. Goods withdrawn for personal use are always recorded at Cost Price (₹14,000), not selling price. Net change = ₹3,20,000 − ₹14,000 = +₹3,06,000.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 2: Meaning and Fundamentals of Double Entry Book-Keeping

questionText: What number is entered in the 'L.F.' (Ledger Folio) column of a Journal?

options.text: The page number of the Ledger on which the relevant account appears
The page number of the Trial Balance schedule
The serial invoice number issued to the customer
The voucher number stored in the Petty Cash file

explanation: L.F. (Ledger Folio) cross-references the exact Ledger page number where each debited or credited account is posted, enabling quick audit verification.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Journal

questionText: In Book-Keeping, what is the concise explanation written in brackets immediately below a journal entry called?

options.text: Folio Note
Contra Endorsement
Narration
Casting Summary

explanation: A Narration is a brief, clear explanation beginning typically with 'Being...' written below every journal entry to state the nature and context of the transaction.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Journal

questionText: When a trader in Pune purchases taxable goods attracting 18% GST from a wholesaler in Nashik (within Maharashtra), which GST accounts are debited in the Journal?

options.text: Output CGST Account at 9% and Output SGST Account at 9%
Input CGST Account at 18% only
Input IGST Account at 18% only
Input CGST Account at 9% and Input SGST Account at 9%

explanation: Intra-state purchases within Maharashtra attract Central GST (Input CGST) and State GST (Input SGST) in equal halves (9% each for an 18% slab).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Journal

questionText: A firm in Mumbai buys a laptop for office use costing ₹50,000 plus 18% GST (intra-state) and pays by cheque. Which journal entry accurately records this transaction?

options.text: Office Equipment/Laptop A/c Dr. ₹50,000; Output CGST A/c Dr. ₹4,500; Output SGST A/c Dr. ₹4,500 — To Cash A/c ₹59,000
Office Equipment/Laptop A/c Dr. ₹50,000; Input CGST A/c Dr. ₹4,500; Input SGST A/c Dr. ₹4,500 — To Bank A/c ₹59,000
Purchases A/c Dr. ₹50,000; Input CGST A/c Dr. ₹4,500; Input SGST A/c Dr. ₹4,500 — To Bank A/c ₹59,000
Office Equipment/Laptop A/c Dr. ₹59,000 — To Bank A/c ₹59,000

explanation: Purchase of an office asset is debited to Laptop/Office Equipment A/c (₹50,000), intra-state 18% GST is split into Input CGST ₹4,500 and Input SGST ₹4,500, and Bank A/c is credited with ₹59,000.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Journal

questionText: ₹8,500 is received in cash from Rohit, whose account had been completely written off as Bad Debts two years ago. Which account should be credited in the Journal?

options.text: Rohit's Personal Account with ₹8,500
Bad Debts Account with ₹8,500
Sundry Debtors Account with ₹8,500
Bad Debts Recovered Account with ₹8,500

explanation: Because Rohit's Personal Account was already closed when written off earlier, the unexpected recovery is a nominal gain credited to Bad Debts Recovered Account (Cash A/c Dr. ₹8,500 To Bad Debts Recovered A/c ₹8,500).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Journal

questionText: Goods costing ₹12,000 (normal selling price ₹15,000) are distributed free of charge as promotional samples. What is the correct journal entry?

options.text: Advertisement A/c Dr. ₹12,000 — To Goods Distributed as Free Samples A/c (or Purchases A/c) ₹12,000
Drawings A/c Dr. ₹12,000 — To Purchases A/c ₹12,000
Free Samples A/c Dr. ₹15,000 — To Stock A/c ₹15,000
Advertisement A/c Dr. ₹15,000 — To Sales A/c ₹15,000

explanation: Promotional distribution of goods is a marketing expense valued at cost price (₹12,000): Advertisement A/c is debited and Goods Distributed as Free Samples A/c (or Purchases A/c) is credited.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Journal

questionText: At the start of the new accounting year, a trader brings forward: Cash ₹25,000, Bank ₹75,000, Stock ₹90,000, Debtors ₹60,000, Machinery ₹1,50,000, Sundry Creditors ₹85,000, and Bank Loan ₹65,000. What amount is credited to Capital Account in the Opening Entry?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Journal

topic: Partial Cash Settlement with Trade and Cash Discount
questionText: Goods of list price ₹1,00,000 are sold to Priya at 15% trade discount and 4% cash discount. Priya pays 50% of the net invoice amount immediately in cash and keeps the remaining 50% on credit. Which compound journal entry correctly records this sale?

options.text: Cash A/c Dr. ₹39,100; Discount Allowed A/c Dr. ₹3,400; Priya's A/c Dr. ₹42,500 — To Sales A/c ₹85,000
Cash A/c Dr. ₹40,800; Discount Allowed A/c Dr. ₹1,700; Priya's A/c Dr. ₹42,500 — To Sales A/c ₹85,000
Cash A/c Dr. ₹40,800; Discount Allowed A/c Dr. ₹19,200; Priya's A/c Dr. ₹40,000 — To Sales A/c ₹1,00,000
Cash A/c Dr. ₹42,500; Priya's A/c Dr. ₹42,500 — To Sales A/c ₹81,600; To Discount Received A/c ₹3,400

explanation: Net invoice after 15% trade discount = ₹85,000. Credit half debited to Priya's A/c = ₹42,500. Cash half = ₹42,500 less 4% cash discount (₹1,700) = ₹40,800 cash received.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Journal

topic: Goods Destroyed by Fire with Partial Insurance Claim
questionText: Warehouse stock costing ₹60,000 is destroyed by fire, and the insurance company admits a claim for 70% of the loss. How is this recorded in the Journal?

options.text: Insurance Company A/c Dr. ₹42,000; Loss by Fire A/c Dr. ₹18,000 — To Goods Destroyed by Fire A/c ₹60,000
Insurance Company A/c Dr. ₹60,000 — To Goods Destroyed by Fire A/c ₹42,000; To Profit & Loss A/c ₹18,000
Bank A/c Dr. ₹42,000; Repairs A/c Dr. ₹18,000 — To Sales A/c ₹60,000
Loss by Fire A/c Dr. ₹60,000 — To Insurance Company A/c ₹42,000; To Purchases A/c ₹18,000

explanation: Admitted claim (70% of ₹60,000 = ₹42,000) is receivable from the insurer (Insurance Co. A/c Dr.), the uncovered ₹18,000 is an abnormal loss (Loss by Fire A/c Dr.), and ₹60,000 is credited to Goods Destroyed by Fire A/c.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Journal

questionText: An old machine having a book value of ₹45,000 is exchanged at an agreed trade-in value of ₹32,000 against the purchase of a new machine priced at ₹1,20,000, and the balance is paid by cheque. What cheque payment and loss are recorded?

options.text: Bank A/c credited ₹1,20,000 and Old Machinery A/c credited ₹32,000
Bank A/c credited ₹75,000 and Loss on Exchange of Machinery A/c debited ₹13,000
Bank A/c credited ₹88,000 and Profit on Exchange of Machinery A/c credited ₹13,000
Bank A/c credited ₹88,000 and Loss on Exchange of Machinery A/c debited ₹13,000

explanation: Loss on trade-in = Book value ₹45,000 − Exchange value ₹32,000 = ₹13,000 (debited). Balance payable by cheque = ₹1,20,000 − ₹32,000 = ₹88,000 (credited to Bank A/c). Total debits (₹1,20,000 + ₹13,000) equal total credits (₹45,000 + ₹88,000 = ₹1,33,000).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 3: Journal

topic: Meaning of Debit Balance in Ledger
questionText: When balancing a T-format Ledger account at month-end, if the Debit side total exceeds the Credit side total, what type of balance does the account have and where is the closing 'Balance c/d' written?

options.text: Credit balance — written as 'By Balance c/d' on the Credit side
Debit balance — written as 'To Balance c/d' on the Debit side
Zero balance — transferred immediately to Suspense Account
Debit balance — written as 'By Balance c/d' on the Credit side to equalise totals

explanation: An account shows a Debit balance whenever Debit total > Credit total. To equalise both columns while closing, 'By Balance c/d' is inserted on the lighter Credit side and brought down as 'To Balance b/d' on the Debit side.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Ledger

questionText: How are Nominal Accounts such as Salaries Account or Commission Received Account closed at the end of the financial year?

options.text: By transferring them directly to the Capital Account in the Journal
By transferring their totals to the Trading Account or Profit and Loss Account without carrying forward balances
By posting them to the Suspense Account in the Balance Sheet
By inserting 'By Balance c/d' and carrying their balances to next year's Opening Entry

explanation: Nominal accounts measure periodic expenses, losses, incomes, and gains for a single accounting period; they are closed into Trading or Profit & Loss A/c rather than carried forward.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Ledger

questionText: Why can the Cash Account (Cash in Hand) in the Ledger never show a Credit balance?

options.text: Because Cash Account is closed directly to Trading Account
Because Cash Account is an Artificial Personal Account
Because physical cash payments can never exceed cash available in hand
Because cash receipts are always posted on the Credit side

explanation: Cash Account is a tangible Real Account: cash inflows are debited and outflows credited. Since a business cannot physically pay out more currency than it holds, Cash A/c has either a Debit balance or nil balance.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Ledger

questionText: In Sanket's (Debtor) Ledger Account for April: Opening debit balance ₹24,000; Credit sales ₹68,000; Sanket's dishonoured cheque ₹8,000; Cheques received from Sanket ₹55,000; Discount allowed ₹2,000; Sales returns ₹5,000. What is Sanket's closing balance?

options.text: ₹38,000 Debit balance
₹22,000 Debit balance
₹42,000 Debit balance
₹38,000 Credit balance

explanation: Debit side of Debtor's A/c = Opening ₹24,000 + Credit sales ₹68,000 + Dishonoured cheque ₹8,000 = ₹1,00,000. Credit side = ₹55,000 + ₹2,000 + ₹5,000 = ₹62,000. Closing Debit balance = ₹1,00,000 − ₹62,000 = ₹38,000.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Ledger

questionText: How is the compound entry 'Cash A/c Dr. ₹19,400; Discount Allowed A/c Dr. ₹600 — To Swapnil's A/c ₹20,000' posted into Swapnil's Ledger Account?

options.text: On the Credit side as 'By Cash A/c ₹20,000' only
On the Credit side as 'By Cash A/c ₹19,400' and 'By Discount Allowed A/c ₹600'
On the Credit side as 'By Swapnil's A/c ₹20,000'
On the Debit side as 'To Cash A/c ₹19,400' and 'To Discount Allowed A/c ₹600'

explanation: Swapnil's A/c is credited for ₹20,000 in total, so posting goes to its Credit side referencing the two corresponding debited accounts: 'By Cash A/c ₹19,400' and 'By Discount Allowed A/c ₹600'.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Ledger

questionText: While preparing a Trial Balance under the Balance Method from Ledger accounts, which of the following ledger balances is placed in the Credit column?

options.text: Carriage Outwards Account
Drawings Account
Return Outwards (Purchase Return) Account
Return Inwards (Sales Return) Account

explanation: Return Outwards represents goods returned to suppliers, reducing Purchases, and carries a Credit balance. Drawings, Return Inwards, and Carriage Outwards all carry Debit balances.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Ledger

topic: Posting Subsidiary Book Totals to Ledger
questionText: At the end of July, the Purchases Book shows a monthly total of ₹1,48,000 across 12 credit invoices. How is this posted to the Purchases Account in the Ledger?

options.text: Credited once at month-end as 'By Sundries as per Purchases Book ₹1,48,000'
Posted only to individual suppliers' accounts while Purchases Account is left blank
Transferred directly to Balance Sheet without entering the Ledger
Debited once at month-end as 'To Sundries as per Purchases Book ₹1,48,000'

explanation: Individual credit invoices are credited daily to respective suppliers' Personal Accounts, while the monthly total of Purchases Book is debited in a single lump sum to Purchases Account as 'To Sundries as per Purchases Book'.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Ledger

topic: Finding Missing Capital in Trial Balance
questionText: A trader's ledger balances on 31st March are: Machinery ₹1,80,000; Debtors ₹74,000; Creditors ₹52,000; Purchases ₹2,10,000; Sales ₹3,15,000; Return Inwards ₹9,000; Return Outwards ₹6,000; Bank Overdraft ₹28,000; Opening Stock ₹42,000; Salaries ₹36,000; Drawings ₹15,000; and Capital (?). What is the Capital balance that makes the Trial Balance tally?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Ledger

questionText: M/s Joshi Traders (Creditor) had an opening credit balance of ₹45,000 on 1st May. During May: credit purchases from them ₹92,000; defective goods returned to them ₹7,000; Bills Payable accepted in their favour ₹50,000; cash paid to them ₹38,500; discount received from them ₹1,500. How is the closing balance shown on 31st May?

options.text: Credit balance of ₹54,000 — entered as 'To Balance c/d ₹54,000' on the Debit side while closing
Credit balance of ₹40,000 — entered as 'By Balance c/d ₹40,000' on the Credit side while closing
Credit balance of ₹40,000 — entered as 'To Balance c/d ₹40,000' on the Debit side while closing
Debit balance of ₹40,000 — entered as 'By Balance c/d ₹40,000' on the Credit side while closing

explanation: Credit total = ₹45,000 + ₹92,000 = ₹1,37,000. Debit entries = ₹7,000 + ₹50,000 + ₹38,500 + ₹1,500 = ₹97,000. Net Credit balance = ₹40,000, entered as 'To Balance c/d ₹40,000' on the Debit side to balance the T-account.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Ledger

topic: Total Method vs Balance Method of Trial Balance
questionText: A firm's Trial Balance under the Balance Method tallies at ₹3,85,000. Only two Ledger accounts had entries on both sides: Cash A/c (Debit total ₹2,40,000; Credit total ₹1,95,000) and Debtors A/c (Debit total ₹1,10,000; Credit total ₹70,000). What will be the grand total of each column if the Trial Balance is prepared under the Total Method instead?
explanation: Under the Balance Method, netting removes min(Dr, Cr) from both sides of each two-sided account (₹1,95,000 for Cash and ₹70,000 for Debtors). Restoring gross totals adds ₹1,95,000 + ₹70,000 = ₹2,65,000 to each column: ₹3,85,000 + ₹2,65,000 = ₹6,50,000.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 4: Ledger

topic: Source Document for Purchase Return Book
questionText: Which source document is prepared and sent by a buyer to a supplier when returning defective goods bought on credit?

options.text: Debit Note
Cash Memo
Pay-in-Slip
Credit Note

explanation: When returning goods bought on credit, the purchaser debits the supplier's account to reduce liability and issues a Debit Note stating the value and reason for return.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Subsidiary Books

questionText: A cloth merchant buys Wooden Display Racks worth ₹35,000 on credit from Metro Furniture Mart for showroom use. In which book of original entry is this recorded?

options.text: Petty Cash Book
Purchases Book
Two-Column Cash Book
Journal Proper

explanation: Purchases Book records ONLY credit purchases of trading goods meant for resale. Credit purchase of fixed assets (display racks for a cloth merchant) is recorded in Journal Proper.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Subsidiary Books

topic: Contra Entries in Two-Column Cash Book
questionText: What does the letter 'C' written in the Ledger Folio column of a Two-Column Cash Book signify?

options.text: Credit sale verified by the head cashier
Contra entry affecting both Cash and Bank columns simultaneously, requiring no separate Ledger posting
Cancelled cheque excluded from Cash Book totals
Commission deducted at source by the bank

explanation: A Contra entry ('C') indicates that both debit and credit aspects (Cash and Bank columns) are completed inside the Two-Column Cash Book itself, so neither requires posting to the Ledger.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Subsidiary Books

questionText: Which of the following transactions is NOT recorded as a Contra entry in a Two-Column Cash Book (Cash and Bank columns)?

options.text: Cash withdrawn from bank for office expenses
A bearer cheque received on Monday (entered in Cash column) and deposited into bank on Thursday
Cash withdrawn from bank for the proprietor's household use
Cash deposited into the business bank account

explanation: Withdrawing cash from bank for personal/household use is debited to Drawings Account and credited to Bank column only—it never enters office cash, so it is not a Contra entry.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Subsidiary Books

topic: Imprest System of Petty Cash Book
questionText: Under the Imprest System, the Head Cashier gives an imprest float of ₹5,000 to the Petty Cashier on 1st April. During the week, the Petty Cashier pays ₹1,150 for postage, ₹980 for conveyance, ₹740 for stationery, and ₹630 for carriage. How much cash is reimbursed on 8th April to restore the imprest?
explanation: Total petty expenditure = ₹1,150 + ₹980 + ₹740 + ₹630 = ₹3,500 (leaving ₹1,500 cash balance). Under the Imprest System, exact expenditure (₹3,500) is reimbursed so the float returns to ₹5,000.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Subsidiary Books

topic: Bearer Cheque Treatment in Cash Book
questionText: A firm receives a bearer cheque of ₹15,000 from customer Neha on 10th June and retains it in the office safe before depositing it into the bank on 14th June. How is this treated in a Two-Column Cash Book?

options.text: Recorded directly in Bank column (Dr.) on 10th June with no entry on 14th June
Recorded in Cash column (Dr.) on 10th June, followed by a Contra entry depositing ₹15,000 from Cash to Bank on 14th June
Recorded in Journal Proper on 10th June and Sales Book on 14th June
Ignored on 10th June and recorded only after bank realisation

explanation: In MSBSHSE accounting practice, an undeposited bearer cheque is treated like cash in hand on receipt date (10th June, Cash Dr.) and recorded as a Contra deposit (Bank Dr. To Cash Cr.) when banked on 14th June.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Subsidiary Books

questionText: An electrical dealer had four transactions in August: (1) Sold on credit to Kulkarni Stores: 20 fans @ ₹2,500 each less 10% trade discount; (2) Sold for cash to Deshmukh: 10 mixers @ ₹3,000 each; (3) Sold old office printer on credit to Rane for ₹4,000; (4) Sold on credit to Patil Agencies: 15 irons @ ₹1,200 each less 5% trade discount. What is the monthly total of the Sales Book?
explanation: Only credit sales of trading goods enter Sales Book: (1) 20 × ₹2,500 − 10% = ₹45,000; (4) 15 × ₹1,200 − 5% = ₹17,100. Cash sales (₹30,000) go to Cash Book and asset sale (₹4,000) goes to Journal Proper. Total = ₹45,000 + ₹17,100 = ₹62,100.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Subsidiary Books

topic: Two-Column Cash Book with Opening Overdraft
questionText: On 1st March, a Cash Book shows Cash in Hand ₹18,000 (Dr.) and Bank Overdraft ₹42,000 (Cr.). During March: cheques deposited into bank ₹65,000; cash deposited into bank ₹12,000; cheques issued to suppliers ₹24,000; bank charges debited ₹800. What is the closing balance of the Bank column on 31st March?

options.text: ₹1,800 Credit (Overdraft) balance
₹10,200 Credit (Overdraft) balance
₹94,200 Debit (Favourable) balance
₹10,200 Debit (Favourable) balance

explanation: Bank Debit side = ₹65,000 + ₹12,000 = ₹77,000. Bank Credit side = Opening Overdraft ₹42,000 + Cheques issued ₹24,000 + Bank charges ₹800 = ₹66,800. Since Debit exceeds Credit by ₹10,200, closing balance is a favourable Debit balance of ₹10,200.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Subsidiary Books

questionText: Up to 31st March, the Cash column of a Two-Column Cash Book shows gross receipts (including opening cash) of ₹94,500 and cash payments of ₹58,200. The proprietor instructs: 'Retain ₹10,000 cash in hand and deposit the entire excess into the Bank.' What amount is entered as the Contra bank deposit?
explanation: Cash available before bank deposit = ₹94,500 − ₹58,200 = ₹36,300. Retaining ₹10,000 as closing cash in hand leaves ₹36,300 − ₹10,000 = ₹26,300 to be deposited into Bank via Contra entry.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Subsidiary Books

questionText: Consider five March transactions: (i) Credit purchase of trading goods ₹30,000; (ii) Goods costing ₹6,000 withdrawn by proprietor for personal use; (iii) Irrecoverable debt of ₹4,500 written off; (iv) Credit purchase of office computer ₹48,000; (v) Return of damaged goods to supplier ₹3,000. What is the aggregate value of entries recorded in Journal Proper?
explanation: Item (i) goes to Purchases Book and (v) to Purchase Return Book. Items (ii) ₹6,000, (iii) ₹4,500, and (iv) ₹48,000 have no special subsidiary book and enter Journal Proper: ₹6,000 + ₹4,500 + ₹48,000 = ₹58,500.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 5: Subsidiary Books

topic: Cash Book vs Pass Book Balances
questionText: A favourable (Debit) balance in the Bank column of a trader's Cash Book corresponds to which balance in the Bank Pass Book?

options.text: Suspense balance as per Pass Book
Debit balance as per Pass Book
Credit balance as per Pass Book
Overdraft balance as per Pass Book

explanation: Deposits held by the bank represent an asset to the trader (Debit in Cash Book) and a liability owed by the bank to its customer (Credit in Pass Book).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Bank Reconciliation Statement

questionText: Who prepares a Bank Reconciliation Statement and for what primary purpose?

options.text: The account holder (business enterprise) to reconcile differences between the Cash Book Bank column and the Pass Book
The Reserve Bank of India during statutory bank audits
The bank branch manager to calculate annual interest on savings accounts
Sundry creditors to verify trade discount settlements

explanation: A Bank Reconciliation Statement is prepared periodically by the account holder/customer to explain timing and recording differences between the Cash Book (Bank column) and Bank Pass Book.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Bank Reconciliation Statement

questionText: When starting a Bank Reconciliation Statement with a favourable (Debit) balance as per Cash Book, how are 'cheques issued to suppliers but not yet presented for payment' treated?

options.text: Ignored completely because payment was authorised
Debited to Profit and Loss Account
Deducted from the Cash Book balance
Added to the Cash Book balance

explanation: Issuing cheques reduced the Cash Book balance immediately, whereas the Pass Book has not yet been debited; hence they are added back to arrive at the higher Pass Book balance.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Bank Reconciliation Statement

topic: BRS from Favourable Cash Book Balance
questionText: On 31st March 2026, a trader's Cash Book shows a Debit bank balance of ₹48,000. On scrutiny: (i) Cheques issued but not presented ₹14,500; (ii) Cheques deposited into bank but not yet cleared ₹19,200; (iii) Dividend collected directly by bank ₹3,700; (iv) Bank charges entered in Pass Book only ₹500. What is the balance as per Pass Book?

options.text: ₹43,300 (Credit)
₹46,500 (Credit)
₹50,500 (Credit)
₹49,500 (Credit)

explanation: Pass Book balance = ₹48,000 + ₹14,500 (unpresented) − ₹19,200 (uncleared) + ₹3,700 (dividend) − ₹500 (charges) = ₹46,500 favourable (Credit) balance.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Bank Reconciliation Statement

questionText: Overdraft (Credit balance) as per Cash Book on 30th June is ₹35,000. Adjustments: (i) Cheques deposited into bank ₹11,000 not yet collected; (ii) Cheques issued ₹8,400 not yet presented; (iii) Interest on overdraft ₹1,900 debited in Pass Book only; (iv) Customer directly deposited ₹6,500 into bank. Find the Overdraft as per Pass Book.
explanation: Starting with Cash Book Overdraft ₹35,000: Add items increasing overdraft (+₹11,000 uncollected cheques + ₹1,900 interest = ₹12,900) and Less items reducing overdraft (−₹8,400 unpresented cheques − ₹6,500 direct deposit = −₹14,900). Pass Book Overdraft = ₹35,000 + ₹12,900 − ₹14,900 = ₹33,000.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Bank Reconciliation Statement

topic: BRS from Favourable Pass Book Balance
questionText: Credit balance as per Pass Book on 31st March is ₹62,000. (i) A deposited cheque of ₹9,000 was dishonoured in Pass Book, not yet recorded in Cash Book; (ii) Out of cheques of ₹15,000 issued in March, cheques worth ₹6,000 were presented in April; (iii) Bank paid ₹2,500 insurance premium under standing instructions (unrecorded in Cash Book). Find the Debit balance as per Cash Book.
explanation: Starting from Pass Book (Cr.) ₹62,000: Add dishonoured cheque (+₹9,000) and standing-order payment (+₹2,500) where Cash Book is still higher; Less unpresented March cheques (−₹6,000) already deducted in Cash Book. Cash Book balance = ₹62,000 + ₹9,000 + ₹2,500 − ₹6,000 = ₹67,500.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Bank Reconciliation Statement

questionText: Cheques totalling ₹42,000 were issued to creditors during March 2026, out of which cheques amounting to ₹29,500 were encashed at the bank on or before 31st March 2026. When preparing BRS as on 31st March 2026 starting with a Debit balance as per Cash Book, what adjustment is made?

options.text: Deduct ₹12,500

explanation: Cheques already encashed by 31st March (₹29,500) appear in both books. Only the unpresented difference (₹42,000 − ₹29,500 = ₹12,500) causes discrepancy and is added to Cash Book balance.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Bank Reconciliation Statement

questionText: Starting with a favourable (Debit) balance as per Cash Book of ₹54,000, you discover that a cheque of ₹7,500 issued to supplier Sharma was mistakenly entered on the Debit (Receipt) side of the Cash Book Bank column instead of the Credit (Payment) side, whereas the bank duly honoured it. What is the Pass Book balance (assuming no other differences)?

options.text: ₹46,500 (Credit)
₹39,000 (Credit)
₹61,500 (Credit)
₹69,000 (Credit)

explanation: Honouring the cheque reduced the true bank balance by ₹7,500, whereas debiting it in Cash Book inflated Cash Book by ₹7,500—creating a double error of ₹15,000. Pass Book balance = ₹54,000 − ₹15,000 = ₹39,000.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Bank Reconciliation Statement

topic: Pass Book Overdraft with Dishonoured Bill and Undercasting
questionText: On 31st March 2026, Pass Book shows an Overdraft (Debit balance) of ₹28,000. Scrutiny reveals: (i) Receipt (Debit) side of Cash Book Bank column was undercast by ₹3,000; (ii) A Bill Receivable of ₹12,000 previously discounted with the bank (discount ₹400) was dishonoured on 30th March and bank paid ₹200 noting charges (unrecorded in Cash Book); (iii) Cheques deposited ₹9,500 remain uncollected. What was the balance as per Cash Book?

options.text: Favourable (Debit balance) of ₹9,300
Overdraft (Credit balance) of ₹15,300
Overdraft (Credit balance) of ₹9,900
Overdraft (Credit balance) of ₹9,300

explanation: Let signed Cash Book balance be CB. Undercasting Dr. side makes PB ₹3,000 higher (+₹3,000); dishonoured bill is debited at full face value plus noting charges (−₹12,200, ignoring old discount); uncollected cheques (−₹9,500). Thus −₹28,000 = CB + ₹3,000 − ₹12,200 − ₹9,500 = CB − ₹18,700 ⇒ CB = −₹9,300 (Overdraft ₹9,300).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Bank Reconciliation Statement

questionText: A trader's Cash Book shows a favourable Debit balance of ₹16,000 on 31st December. Cheques of ₹31,000 deposited in late December were not cleared, cheques of ₹8,000 issued were not presented, bank debited ₹1,200 charges, and a customer directly deposited ₹3,200. What balance is shown by the Pass Book?

options.text: Favourable (Credit balance) of ₹27,000
Favourable (Credit balance) of ₹5,000
Overdraft (Debit balance) of ₹5,000
Overdraft (Debit balance) of ₹9,000

explanation: Signed Pass Book position = +₹16,000 − ₹31,000 (uncleared) + ₹8,000 (unpresented) − ₹1,200 (charges) + ₹3,200 (direct deposit) = −₹5,000. Because the result is negative, the Pass Book shows an Overdraft (Debit balance) of ₹5,000.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 6: Bank Reconciliation Statement

questionText: Under the Fixed Instalment (Straight Line) Method, how is annual depreciation computed when no percentage rate is specified?

options.text: (Original Cost of Asset + Estimated Scrap Value) ÷ Estimated Useful Life in Years
(Original Cost of Asset − Estimated Scrap Value) ÷ Estimated Useful Life in Years
(Market Value of Asset − Installation Charges) × Useful Life
Opening Written Down Value ÷ Remaining Life without deducting Scrap Value

explanation: Fixed Instalment Method spreads the depreciable cost (Original Cost including installation minus Estimated Residual/Scrap Value) equally across the asset's estimated useful life.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Depreciation

questionText: Under the Written Down Value (Diminishing Balance) Method of depreciation, what happens to the annual depreciation charge and book value over successive years?

options.text: Annual depreciation increases every year due to compounding
Depreciation is charged only in years when net profit is earned
Annual depreciation decreases each year and the asset's book value never becomes completely zero
Annual depreciation remains constant every year until book value reaches zero

explanation: Because a fixed percentage is applied each year to the declining opening book balance rather than original cost, annual depreciation diminishes progressively and never reduces the asset to zero.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Depreciation

questionText: When an existing computer server loses economic value because a far faster generation of processors enters the market—despite the server still functioning physically—which cause of depreciation is operating?

options.text: Obsolescence
Amortisation of goodwill
Depletion
Physical wear and tear

explanation: Obsolescence refers to loss of usefulness of an asset arising from technological innovation, new inventions, or shifts in market demand rather than physical deterioration.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Depreciation

questionText: A firm buys machinery for ₹2,15,000 and pays ₹25,000 for freight and erection. Its estimated scrap value at the end of a 7-year useful life is ₹30,000. What is the annual depreciation under the Fixed Instalment Method?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Depreciation

questionText: Equipment costing ₹1,60,000 is purchased on 1st October 2024. Depreciation is charged @ 10% p.a. under the Written Down Value Method and accounts close on 31st March every year. What is the depreciation for the second financial year (FY 2025-26)?
explanation: FY 2024-25 depreciation for 6 months (1 Oct 2024 to 31 Mar 2025) = ₹1,60,000 × 10% × 6/12 = ₹8,000. Opening WDV on 1st April 2025 = ₹1,52,000. Full-year depreciation for FY 2025-26 = 10% of ₹1,52,000 = ₹15,200.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Depreciation

topic: Loss on Asset Disposal under SLM
questionText: A delivery van purchased on 1st April 2023 for ₹5,00,000 is depreciated @ 15% p.a. under the Fixed Instalment Method (financial year ends 31st March). On 30th September 2025, it is sold for ₹2,95,000. What is the profit or loss on sale?

options.text: Loss on sale of ₹17,500
Profit on sale of ₹17,500
Profit on sale of ₹20,000
Loss on sale of ₹55,000

syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Depreciation

questionText: Even when no cash leaves the enterprise at year-end, how is the balance of Depreciation Account closed on 31st March?

options.text: Carried forward as a Debit balance in next year's Trial Balance
Transferred to the Debit side of Profit and Loss Account
Transferred to the Credit side of Trading Account
Debited directly to Sundry Creditors Account

explanation: Depreciation is a non-cash nominal expense that must be matched against current-year revenue by closing it into the Debit side of the Profit and Loss Account.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Depreciation

topic: Partial Disposal of Machinery under WDV
questionText: On 1st April 2023, a factory bought two identical machines for ₹1,00,000 each (total ₹2,00,000) and charged depreciation @ 20% p.a. on the Written Down Value Method (year ending 31st March). On 1st October 2025, ONE of the machines was sold for ₹62,000. Find the profit or loss on the machine sold.

options.text: Profit on sale of ₹12,000
Loss on sale of ₹4,400
Profit on sale of ₹4,400
Loss on sale of ₹2,000

explanation: Tracking the sold machine (cost ₹1,00,000): WDV on 1 Apr 2024 = ₹80,000; WDV on 1 Apr 2025 = ₹64,000; 6 months' depreciation to 1 Oct 2025 = ₹64,000 × 20% × 6/12 = ₹6,400. Book value on sale date = ₹57,600. Sale for ₹62,000 yields Profit of ₹4,400.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Depreciation

questionText: On 1st April 2025, Plant Account stood at a book value of ₹2,40,000 (Original Cost ₹3,00,000). Additional plant was purchased on 1st July 2025 for ₹1,20,000 and on 1st January 2026 for ₹80,000. If depreciation is charged @ 10% p.a. on Original Cost (year ending 31st March 2026), what is total depreciation for FY 2025-26?
explanation: Under Original Cost (SLM), old plant is depreciated on ₹3,00,000 (not WDV ₹2,40,000) = ₹30,000; 1st July addition for 9 months = ₹1,20,000 × 10% × 9/12 = ₹9,000; 1st Jan addition for 3 months = ₹80,000 × 10% × 3/12 = ₹2,000. Total = ₹41,000.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Depreciation

questionText: A CNC lathe purchased on 1st April 2024 for ₹2,50,000 has a Written Down Value of ₹1,60,000 on 31st March 2026 after two full years of Diminishing Balance depreciation. What annual percentage rate of depreciation was charged?
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 7: Depreciation

questionText: Wages of ₹15,000 paid to technicians for installing a newly purchased boiler were debited to Wages Account instead of Boiler/Machinery Account. What type of accounting error is this?

options.text: Error of Casting
Compensating Error
Error of Complete Omission
Error of Principle

explanation: Treating a Capital Expenditure (asset installation cost) as a Revenue Expenditure violates fundamental accounting principles, making it an Error of Principle.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Rectification of Errors

questionText: Which of the following errors WILL cause a mismatch between the Debit and Credit totals of a Trial Balance?

options.text: Posting a credit sale to Ramesh's Account instead of Rajesh's Account
Undercasting the monthly total of the Sales Return Book by ₹2,400
Completely omitting a credit purchase invoice of ₹9,000 from the Purchases Book
Debiting Repairs to Machinery ₹3,000 to Machinery Account

explanation: Undercasting a subsidiary book is a one-sided Error of Commission affecting only the Sales Return Account in the Ledger, thereby causing the Trial Balance to disagree.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Rectification of Errors

questionText: When a Trial Balance fails to tally despite preliminary checks and Final Accounts must be prepared urgently, where is the temporary difference placed?

options.text: Capital Reserve Account
Profit and Loss Adjustment Account
Suspense Account
Drawing Account

explanation: A Suspense Account temporarily absorbs the net Trial Balance difference—placed on whichever side is shorter—until the underlying one-sided errors are located and rectified.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Rectification of Errors

questionText: Credit sale of goods worth ₹5,400 to Aditi was mistakenly entered in the Sales Book as ₹4,500. What journal entry rectifies this error?

options.text: Aditi's A/c Dr. ₹900 — To Sales A/c ₹900
Aditi's A/c Dr. ₹5,400 — To Suspense A/c ₹5,400
Suspense A/c Dr. ₹900 — To Sales A/c ₹900
Sales A/c Dr. ₹900 — To Aditi's A/c ₹900

explanation: Entering ₹4,500 instead of ₹5,400 in the book of original entry under-recorded both Aditi's A/c (Dr.) and Sales A/c (Cr.) by ₹900; debiting Aditi ₹900 and crediting Sales ₹900 rectifies both.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Rectification of Errors

questionText: Routine whitewashing and minor repairs to an existing office building costing ₹8,000 were wrongly debited to Building Account. Which entry rectifies the error?

options.text: Building A/c Dr. ₹16,000 — To Cash A/c ₹16,000
Building A/c Dr. ₹8,000 — To Repairs A/c ₹8,000
Repairs A/c Dr. ₹8,000 — To Building A/c ₹8,000
Repairs A/c Dr. ₹8,000 — To Suspense A/c ₹8,000

explanation: Routine maintenance is Revenue Expenditure. Debiting Repairs A/c ₹8,000 records the true expense while crediting Building A/c ₹8,000 cancels the wrongful capitalisation.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Rectification of Errors

questionText: Credit purchase of goods worth ₹12,000 from Varun was mistakenly passed through the Sales Book. Which rectifying journal entry corrects the accounts?

options.text: Purchases A/c Dr. ₹12,000 — To Sales A/c ₹12,000
Varun's A/c Dr. ₹24,000 — To Purchases A/c ₹12,000; To Sales A/c ₹12,000
Purchases A/c Dr. ₹12,000 — To Varun's A/c ₹12,000
Purchases A/c Dr. ₹12,000; Sales A/c Dr. ₹12,000 — To Varun's A/c ₹24,000

explanation: Sales A/c was wrongly credited ₹12,000 (debit Sales ₹12,000 to cancel), Purchases A/c was omitted (debit Purchases ₹12,000), and Varun was wrongly debited ₹12,000 instead of credited ₹12,000 (credit Varun ₹24,000).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Rectification of Errors

questionText: After transferring a Trial Balance difference to Suspense Account, it is found that the Sales Book was overcast by ₹3,500. What is the rectifying entry?

options.text: Sundry Debtors A/c Dr. ₹3,500 — To Sales A/c ₹3,500
Sales A/c Dr. ₹3,500 — To Suspense A/c ₹3,500
Sales A/c Dr. ₹7,000 — To Suspense A/c ₹7,000
Suspense A/c Dr. ₹3,500 — To Sales A/c ₹3,500

explanation: Overcasting the Sales Book inflated the Credit balance of Sales Account alone by ₹3,500; debiting Sales A/c ₹3,500 and crediting Suspense A/c ₹3,500 eliminates the excess credit.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Rectification of Errors

questionText: A Trial Balance difference was placed in Suspense Account. Subsequently, rectifying all three existing errors completely closed the Suspense Account: (1) Purchases Book was undercast by ₹6,000; (2) ₹2,500 received from debtor Nikhil (correctly entered in Cash Book) was posted to the Debit of Nikhil's Account; (3) Return Inwards Book was overcast by ₹1,800. What was the original balance placed in Suspense Account when the Trial Balance disagreed?

options.text: Credit balance of ₹800 (Trial Balance Debit total exceeded Credit total by ₹800)
Credit balance of ₹3,300 (Trial Balance Debit total exceeded Credit total by ₹3,300)
Debit balance of ₹800 (Trial Balance Credit total exceeded Debit total by ₹800)
Debit balance of ₹1,700 (Trial Balance Credit total exceeded Debit total by ₹1,700)

explanation: Rectifying entries give: (1) To Suspense Cr. ₹6,000; (2) Suspense Dr. ₹5,000 (double error: ₹2,500 debited instead of credited); (3) Suspense Dr. ₹1,800. Rectification debits to Suspense (₹6,800) exceed credits (₹6,000) by ₹800, so Suspense originally opened with a Credit balance of ₹800.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Rectification of Errors

topic: Impact of Errors on Net Profit
questionText: Draft Net Profit before rectification is ₹1,15,000. Three errors are discovered: (1) Office furniture bought for ₹20,000 at start of year was debited to Purchases A/c (and 10% p.a. depreciation on furniture was omitted); (2) Discount Received of ₹1,400 was posted to the Debit of Discount Allowed A/c; (3) Credit sale of ₹6,000 to Pranav was entered in Sales Book correctly, but posted to Pranav's A/c as ₹600. Find the corrected Net Profit.
explanation: Error (1) removes ₹20,000 from Purchases (+₹20,000) and charges 10% depreciation (−₹2,000), net +₹18,000. Error (2) cancels wrong debit AND records omitted credit (+₹2,800). Error (3) affects only Personal A/c & Suspense (₹0 P&L impact). Corrected Net Profit = ₹1,15,000 + ₹18,000 + ₹2,800 = ₹1,35,800.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Rectification of Errors

topic: Compensating Errors Effect on Gross Profit
questionText: Suppose the Purchases Book is undercast by ₹4,200 and in the same month the Sales Book is also undercast by ₹4,200. Before rectification, how do these errors affect the Trial Balance and Gross Profit?

options.text: Trial Balance still tallies, but Gross Profit is understated by ₹4,200
Trial Balance disagrees by ₹4,200 and Gross Profit is unaffected
Trial Balance disagrees by ₹8,400 and Gross Profit is overstated by ₹8,400
Trial Balance still tallies, and net Gross Profit remains unaffected even though both Purchases and Sales are understated by ₹4,200

explanation: Understating Purchases (Dr.) by ₹4,200 and Sales (Cr.) by ₹4,200 forms a Compensating Error so Trial Balance tallies. In Trading Account, ₹4,200 lower debit offsets ₹4,200 lower credit, leaving Gross Profit unchanged.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 8: Rectification of Errors

chapter: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
questionText: In the Final Accounts of a sole trader, how are 'Carriage Inwards' and 'Carriage Outwards' respectively treated?

options.text: Carriage Inwards is debited to Trading Account; Carriage Outwards is debited to Profit and Loss Account
Both are shown on the Assets side of the Balance Sheet
Both are debited to Trading Account as direct expenses
Carriage Inwards is debited to Profit and Loss Account; Carriage Outwards to Trading Account

explanation: Carriage Inwards is freight on bringing purchases into the godown (direct expense → Trading A/c), whereas Carriage Outwards is delivery freight on goods sold (indirect distribution expense → P&L A/c).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern

chapter: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
questionText: If 'Closing Stock' appears INSIDE the Trial Balance (rather than as an adjustment outside it), where is it recorded in Final Accounts?

options.text: Only once — on the Credit side of the Trading Account
Twice — on Trading Account Credit side and Balance Sheet Assets side
Only once — on the Assets side of the Balance Sheet
Deducted from Capital on the Liabilities side of the Balance Sheet

explanation: Closing Stock inside the Trial Balance means it has already been adjusted against Purchases (Cost of Goods Sold), so it represents an existing asset balance shown solely on the Balance Sheet Assets side.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern

chapter: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
questionText: When a Balance Sheet is marshalled in the 'Order of Liquidity', which asset is listed first at the top of the Assets side?

options.text: Land and Building
Cash in Hand
Plant and Machinery
Goodwill

explanation: Order of Liquidity arranges assets from most readily convertible into cash (Cash in Hand, Cash at Bank, Bills Receivable, Debtors...) down to least liquid fixed/intangible assets (Land, Goodwill).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern

chapter: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
topic: Cost of Goods Sold and Gross Profit
questionText: From the following figures, calculate Gross Profit: Opening Stock ₹45,000; Purchases ₹2,80,000; Purchase Returns ₹12,000; Wages & Octroi ₹22,000; Sales ₹3,90,000; Sales Returns ₹10,000; Closing Stock ₹55,000.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern

chapter: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
topic: Bad Debts and Reserve for Doubtful Debts
questionText: A Trial Balance shows: Sundry Debtors ₹84,000; Bad Debts ₹2,000 (Dr.); Old R.D.D. ₹3,500 (Cr.). Adjustments require writing off Further Bad Debts of ₹4,000 and maintaining New R.D.D. @ 5% on Debtors. What net amount is debited to the Profit and Loss Account?
explanation: Good Debtors = ₹84,000 − ₹4,000 = ₹80,000. New R.D.D. = 5% of ₹80,000 = ₹4,000. Net debit to P&L A/c = Old Bad Debts ₹2,000 + New Bad Debts ₹4,000 + New R.D.D. ₹4,000 − Old R.D.D. ₹3,500 = ₹6,500.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern

chapter: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
questionText: An annual fire insurance premium of ₹24,000 was paid on 1st July 2025 covering the 12 months up to 30th June 2026. When Final Accounts are prepared on 31st March 2026, what amounts go to the Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet?

options.text: ₹18,000 debited to P&L Account and ₹6,000 shown on Assets side as Prepaid Insurance
₹24,000 debited to P&L Account and ₹6,000 shown on Liabilities side
₹16,000 debited to P&L Account and ₹8,000 shown on Assets side
₹6,000 debited to P&L Account and ₹18,000 shown on Assets side

explanation: Nine months (1st July 2025 to 31st March 2026) expire in current FY = ₹18,000 expense; three months (April–June 2026) = ₹24,000 × 3/12 = ₹6,000 Prepaid Insurance asset.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern

chapter: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
questionText: How does accounting convention distinguish 'Wages and Salaries' from 'Salaries and Wages' in Final Accounts?

options.text: Both are divided 50:50 between Trading Account and Balance Sheet
Both are debited to Profit and Loss Account as office expenses
'Wages and Salaries' is debited to Profit and Loss Account, whereas 'Salaries and Wages' goes to Trading Account
'Wages and Salaries' is debited to Trading Account, whereas 'Salaries and Wages' is debited to Profit and Loss Account

explanation: The first-named word indicates dominant nature: 'Wages and Salaries' represents predominantly factory/direct labour (Trading A/c), whereas 'Salaries and Wages' represents predominantly office staff remuneration (P&L A/c).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern

chapter: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
topic: Manager's Commission After Charging Such Commission
questionText: Net Profit of a concern before charging the Manager's Commission is ₹1,32,000. Under his service contract, the Manager is entitled to a commission of 10% on Net Profit remaining AFTER charging such commission. Find the Manager's Commission and final Net Profit.

options.text: Commission ₹13,200 and Final Net Profit ₹1,18,800
Commission ₹11,000 and Final Net Profit ₹1,21,000
Commission ₹12,000 and Final Net Profit ₹1,20,000
Commission ₹14,667 and Final Net Profit ₹1,17,333

explanation: Commission after charging such commission = Profit before commission × [Rate ÷ (100 + Rate)] = ₹1,32,000 × (10 ÷ 110) = ₹12,000. Final Net Profit = ₹1,32,000 − ₹12,000 = ₹1,20,000 (10% of ₹1,20,000 = ₹12,000).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern

chapter: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
topic: Sequential Debtors Provisions in Balance Sheet
questionText: Trial Balance shows Sundry Debtors at ₹1,06,000. Adjustments require: (i) Write off Further Bad Debts ₹6,000; (ii) Provide 5% R.D.D. on Debtors; (iii) Provide 2% Reserve for Discount on Debtors. What net value of Sundry Debtors is reported on the Assets side of the Balance Sheet?
explanation: Step 1: Deduct Further Bad Debts: ₹1,06,000 − ₹6,000 = ₹1,00,000. Step 2: Deduct 5% R.D.D. (₹5,000) = ₹95,000 good solvent debtors. Step 3: Deduct 2% Reserve for Discount on ₹95,000 (₹1,900) = ₹93,100.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern

chapter: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern
questionText: A Trial Balance as on 31st March 2026 contains: '12% Bank Loan (taken on 1st October 2025) ₹2,00,000 (Cr.)' and 'Interest on Bank Loan paid ₹8,000 (Dr.)'. What hidden adjustment must be incorporated in the Final Accounts?

options.text: Outstanding Interest on Bank Loan of ₹4,000 — added to Interest in P&L A/c and shown on Liabilities side
No adjustment is needed since Trial Balance already includes Interest on Bank Loan
Outstanding Interest on Bank Loan of ₹16,000 — added to Interest in P&L A/c and shown on Liabilities side
Prepaid Interest of ₹4,000 — deducted from Interest in P&L A/c and shown on Assets side

explanation: Interest accrued for 6 months (1 Oct 2025 to 31 Mar 2026) = ₹2,00,000 × 12% × 6/12 = ₹12,000. Since only ₹8,000 has been paid, ₹4,000 is Outstanding Interest (added to P&L expense and Liabilities).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 9: Final Accounts of a Proprietary Concern

questionText: Under the Single Entry System, which statement is prepared on the lines of a Balance Sheet to ascertain Opening or Closing Capital?

options.text: Account Current
Trial Balance
Statement of Affairs
Receipts and Payments Account

explanation: Because complete ledger accounts are unavailable under Single Entry, a Statement of Affairs listing estimated/verified assets and external liabilities is prepared to find Capital as the balancing figure.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Single Entry System

questionText: Why is a Joint Stock Company legally barred from maintaining its books under the Single Entry System?

options.text: Single Entry System allows preparation of two Trial Balances simultaneously
The Companies Act, 2013 statutorily mandates accrual-based Double Entry Book-Keeping for all companies
Income Tax authorities treat Single Entry profits as tax-free
Companies have no cash or personal transactions

explanation: Under Section 128 of the Companies Act, 2013, companies must keep books on an accrual basis and according to the Double Entry System; only small sole proprietors/partnerships sometimes use Single Entry.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Single Entry System

topic: Limitation of Single Entry — Arithmetical Accuracy
questionText: Why is it impossible to verify the arithmetical accuracy of books kept under a pure Single Entry System?

options.text: Because Real and Nominal accounts are largely omitted, preventing the preparation of a Trial Balance
Because Opening Capital always equals Closing Capital
Because Personal accounts of debtors and creditors are never maintained
Because Cash Book entries are recorded in foreign currency

explanation: Single Entry records mainly Cash and Personal accounts, omitting one aspect of most transactions; without dual posting across Real and Nominal accounts, a Trial Balance cannot be compiled.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Single Entry System

topic: Profit Determination under Net Worth Method
questionText: A trader maintaining incomplete records had Opening Capital of ₹1,80,000 and Closing Capital of ₹2,45,000. During the year, he withdrew ₹32,000 for personal expenses and introduced ₹50,000 as additional capital. What profit did he earn?
explanation: Adjusted Closing Capital = Closing Capital ₹2,45,000 + Drawings ₹32,000 − Additional Capital ₹50,000 = ₹2,27,000. Profit = ₹2,27,000 − Opening Capital ₹1,80,000 = ₹47,000.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Single Entry System

topic: Closing Capital from Statement of Affairs
questionText: On 31st March 2026, a trader's records show: Cash ₹14,000; Bank Overdraft ₹18,000; Sundry Debtors ₹65,000; Stock ₹80,000; Furniture ₹45,000; Sundry Creditors ₹36,000; Bills Payable ₹12,000. Find Closing Capital from the Statement of Affairs.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Single Entry System

topic: Personal Asset Proceeds and Drawings in Single Entry
questionText: During the year, a proprietor sold her personal gold ornaments for ₹75,000 and invested 80% of the sale proceeds into the business, while paying her son's college tuition of ₹18,000 from the business bank account. How do these items enter the Statement of Profit or Loss?

options.text: Both ₹60,000 and ₹18,000 are added to Opening Capital
Drawings ₹18,000 is deducted from Closing Capital, and Additional Capital ₹75,000 is added
Drawings ₹18,000 is added to Closing Capital, and Additional Capital ₹60,000 is deducted
Drawings ₹18,000 is added to Closing Capital, and Additional Capital ₹75,000 is deducted

explanation: Only the portion actually brought into business (80% of ₹75,000 = ₹60,000) counts as Additional Capital (deducted), while household college fees paid from business funds (₹18,000) is Drawings (added).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Single Entry System

questionText: At year-end, Closing Capital is ₹1,50,000, Drawings during the year were ₹24,000, Additional Capital introduced was ₹30,000, and the Statement of Profit or Loss revealed a Net Loss of ₹16,000. What was the Opening Capital?
explanation: Adjusted Closing Capital = ₹1,50,000 + ₹24,000 − ₹30,000 = ₹1,44,000. Since Adjusted Closing Capital − Opening Capital = −₹16,000 (Loss), Opening Capital = ₹1,44,000 + ₹16,000 = ₹1,60,000.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Single Entry System

topic: Full Statement of Profit or Loss with Adjustments
questionText: Opening Capital on 1st April 2025 was ₹2,00,000 and Closing Capital before adjustments on 31st March 2026 is ₹2,90,000 (including Plant ₹1,20,000 and Debtors ₹50,000). Cash drawings were ₹35,000, goods withdrawn for personal use cost ₹9,000, and Additional Capital of ₹40,000 was introduced on 1st October 2025. Provide: (i) 10% p.a. depreciation on Plant; (ii) 5% R.D.D. on Debtors; (iii) 10% p.a. Interest on Capital. Find final Net Profit.
explanation: Adjusted Closing Capital = ₹2,90,000 + (₹35,000 + ₹9,000 drawings) − ₹40,000 = ₹2,94,000. Profit before adjustments = ₹2,94,000 − ₹2,00,000 = ₹94,000. Deductions: Plant dep. ₹12,000 + R.D.D. ₹2,500 + Interest on Opening Cap (₹20,000) + 6-month Interest on Addl. Cap (₹40,000 × 10% × 6/12 = ₹2,000) = ₹36,500. Net Profit = ₹94,000 − ₹36,500 = ₹57,500.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Single Entry System

topic: Valuation Distortion Across Opening and Closing Statements
questionText: Under Single Entry, suppose an audit reveals that Opening Assets were understated by ₹15,000 while Closing Stock in the Closing Statement of Affairs was overvalued by ₹10,000. How did these two errors jointly distort reported profit before correction?

options.text: Reported profit was understated by ₹25,000
Reported profit was understated by ₹5,000
Reported profit was overstated by ₹25,000
Reported profit was overstated by ₹5,000

explanation: Profit = Adjusted Closing Capital − Opening Capital. Overvaluing Closing Stock inflates Closing Capital (+₹10,000), and understating Opening Assets depresses Opening Capital (−(−₹15,000) = +₹15,000), jointly overstating Profit by ₹25,000.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Single Entry System

topic: Post-Capital Adjustments in Statement of Profit or Loss
questionText: A trader's Profit before adjustments under Single Entry is ₹68,000. Year-end adjustments show: Depreciation on Furniture ₹4,500; Outstanding Salaries ₹5,500; Prepaid Shop Rent ₹3,000; and Interest on Drawings charged to proprietor ₹1,800. What is the Net Profit after adjustments?
explanation: Additions to profit: Prepaid Rent (+₹3,000, an unrecorded asset/expense reduction) and Interest on Drawings (+₹1,800, gain to business) = +₹4,800. Deductions: Depreciation (−₹4,500) and Outstanding Salaries (−₹5,500) = −₹10,000. Net Profit = ₹68,000 + ₹4,800 − ₹10,000 = ₹62,800.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 10: Single Entry System
